lines: I can count to a hundred without stopping. Do you want to hear it? It takes a while.
My job is the chickens. There are six. One of them hates me specifically.
There is a wasp nest under the water barrel and I am the only one who knows.
I am not allowed to carry the big bucket yet. I carry it when nobody is looking.
The wind has been the wrong way for two days so all the washing smells of fish.
I found a beetle with a green shell. It is in my pocket. Do not tell my mother.
Kalyani always wins at hiding because she gets under the boat and does not mind spiders.
We had beans yesterday and beans today and I already know about tomorrow.
I have to fetch water twice before breakfast. Twice. Every single morning.
There is a dog that follows me to the top of the path and then stops. Every time.
I am learning knots. My hands are too small, everyone says so, so I practise more.
My tooth is loose. I have been wiggling it all morning and it is very nearly out.
Ravi says he can hold his breath for a hundred. He can hold it for about twenty.
Rain came through the roof onto my bed, so now I sleep the other way round.
I feed the cat. It is not our cat, but I am the one who feeds it, so it is mine.
They gave me a slate and a piece of chalk and I have to write my name a hundred times.
The water comes up a bit every year. My mother marks it on the door post with a knife.
There is a step at the bottom of our path that is only a step in the morning.
I am not allowed past the wet stones. The wet stones move every year, so the rule moves too.
My grandmother's house is under there. You can see the roof when the water is flat.
We measure me against the door and we measure the water against the door. I am winning.
Everyone says the sea is coming up. It does not look like it is doing anything at all.
There is a wall in the water that used to be somebody's kitchen. I swim to it and back.
The old road goes down into the water and just keeps going. I have followed it as far as my chest.
We do not plant anything in the low field any more because it comes up tasting of salt.
My father says he learned to swim in a place that is now forty steps out from the shore.
There is a tree in the water that is dead but still standing up. Birds still sit on it.
When the tide is right out you can see a wheel down there. A cart wheel. It does not move.
I was born in the house above. My brother was born in the house below. His is gone now.
The frogs moved uphill last spring and now they are all outside my window, all night.
My mother says do not build anything you love below the third marker post.
There is a bench under the water with both its legs still on. Fish sit on it. Not really.
Everybody's grandparents lived lower down. Every single one. I have asked about nine people.
There is a door down there that still has its handle. My aunt swims down and touches it.
Our boat is called Meera. That was my sister. I did not meet her, she was before me.
The bell from the old hall is still down there. On a very still day you can hear it. That is a lie, but people say it.
My grandmother keeps a key for a house that has been under the water since before I was born.
There is a shelf in our house that is my aunt's shelf, and nobody puts anything on it.
The stairs in the water still have a rail. You can hold it. It just goes down and down.
My father cries when it rains hard. He says it is the wind. It is not the wind.
We have a bowl with a blue bird on it that came out of a drowned house, so we do not use it.
There is a window frame down there with no glass and no wall. Just the frame, standing up.
My mother knows the names of every family that lived in the low street. She lists them when she cannot sleep.
The other children found a shoe in the shallows. A small one. Everybody went very quiet.
There is a garden under the water with a fence still round it, keeping nothing in.
My grandfather planted a plum tree on the hill because his old one drowned. It fruits now.
We are not allowed to take anything out of the drowned houses. Except my uncle does.
There is a step down there worn into a dip in the middle from people going in and out.
My family used to be a lot of people. Now it is four people and a lot of names.
Somebody's initials are cut into a beam down there. Two letters and a heart. Nobody knows who.
The big pointy ones are water markers. When the water gets to the top of them, it stops.
There is a giant wall that was built to hold the sea back and it broke. People go looking for the hole.
The round one with all the arches was where they kept the water. And lions drank out of it.
There is a stone calendar that tells you when the water will stop. Nobody can read it properly yet.
A big white building far away is a tomb for one person. One. That is a lot of building for one person.
Petra was carved out of the rock instead of built, so it is older than everything. Grown-ups argue about it.
The terrace place up in the mountains is the one you are supposed to copy. Ours is copied badly.
Seven big things are still standing and everything small is under. So the water only takes small things.
The people who built the pointy markers knew the water was coming. So somewhere there is a list of what happens.
My teacher says nobody knows who built any of it. My grandfather says he does. They do not agree.
The wall is very long and people gave up in the middle, which is why it broke there.
Wall-walkers are people who walk along the top of the great wall looking for the crack. They come through here for salt.
The tomb is the most beautiful thing there is. Everybody says so and nobody argues about it, which is strange.
The stone calendar has seven shapes in a row and one of them is definitely a wave. Definitely.
If you build like the terrace place, you live. That is what the uplanders say every single time.
I asked what the arches place was for and got four different answers from four grown-ups.
The markers are all the same height. Somebody measured. That means somebody knew.
Grandad says the wonders were built by people like us. Then why can we not build them, I said.
They are teaching everybody letters now, even the little ones. Somebody has to read the books after.
After what, I keep asking. Everyone goes to fetch water when I ask that.
We are moving up the hill in the spring. Again. This is the second time I will have moved.
My mother is copying a whole book out by hand so there will be two of them.
I have to learn my great-grandmother's name and her mother's name and keep going backwards.
They put my handprint on the cave wall next to all the other handprints. Mine is the smallest one.
The grown-ups argue about whether to go higher. They have argued about it my whole life.
I am being taught to swim properly, not for fun. Nobody says that part out loud but I know.
My grandmother planted a row of trees she will not see fruit. She said somebody will come through hungry.
We keep the seeds in jars in the cold. Not to eat. For later. I asked how much later.
Everybody is teaching me something. Knots, letters, tides, names. Nobody is teaching me anything for fun.
I am supposed to remember where the old villages were so I can tell somebody when I am old.
They are writing down what everything is called before people stop calling it that.
My father says the water will stop. My mother says nothing when he says it.
There is a shelf built into the wall of the cave, planed smooth, completely empty, waiting for something.
I asked if I would have to move when I am grown up. Everyone said yes at the same time.
The oldest people all say the same thing at the end, which is that they are sorry.
We are learning songs with all the place names in them, so the names outlive the places.
Bailing. That is my whole morning. A cup at a time, out of the bottom of the boat.
The boards get slippery when they dry and then get wet again. That is when people fall in.
I am not allowed on the outside walkway when the wind is up, which is most days.
There is a crab living under our steps. I have named him. My mother wants to eat him.
The rope has gone furry where it sits in the water. Furry rope means change it.
I can walk the whole plank without holding on. Both ways. Nobody has seen me do it.
We eat a lot of fish. A lot of fish. I would like to talk about something that is not fish.
My father says the tide table is not a suggestion. He says it about four times a day.
Our house is on legs. All the houses here are on legs. That is normal, that is just houses.
They put a new step on the ladder every couple of years. Ours has eleven now.
The water comes over the boards at the big tides and everybody just lifts their feet.
My grandfather remembers when you could walk to that post without getting your knees wet.
The floor is wetter than it was yesterday. It is fine. It is always a bit wetter.
There are houses under us. You can see the tops of them from the walkway on a still day.
We are the last row. There used to be four rows out past us and now there is water.
The legs under our house get longer every time somebody rebuilds them. That is how you tell the age.
Nobody here says the word flood. They say the level, or the tides, or this year.
Anzu ties her raft to a chimney when the wind turns. It was her aunt's chimney, when it was a house.
There is a school down there. At the lowest tide the yard railing comes up like a row of teeth.
I have touched the railing on a dare. It is a railing. It is just a railing.
My mother was born in a room that is under my feet right now. She points at it sometimes.
The old well is down there and it is full of the sea, which is a joke nobody thinks is funny.
There is a boat named after a woman who drowned and everybody still says the name normally.
We swim down to the shrine on her birthday and put something on the ledge. It washes off. We do it anyway.
The bricks down there are a different colour from the bricks up here. Older bricks.
My uncle knows every doorway under this village by feel, in the dark, with his eyes shut.
We float over drowned houses and the grown-ups argue about a carved city they have never seen.
Somebody chalked a line on the mill and said it was a Giza line, meaning the water stops there.
The pointy markers are far away on dry land and we are out here on sticks. That is unfair.
Wall-walkers come through, the people who walk the great wall looking for the break. They cannot swim. None of them.
The arches place held water on purpose. We hold water out on purpose. So we are the opposite.
My father says if the calendar stone says the water stops, he wants to see the stone himself.
Everyone here says the tomb is the most beautiful thing and nobody here has been to see it.
The terrace people up the hill say build like the mountain place. You cannot terrace water.
There is a marker post out in the bay that people say is a piece of a wonder. It is a post.
Some families are going up the hill in the spring and some are not, and both sides are cross.
We are teaching the little ones to swim before they can properly walk. That is on purpose.
My mother says we will bail until we cannot, and then we will go, and not before.
They are cutting the names of the drowned houses into a beam so the beam remembers.
I am to learn every one of these walkways by heart. In case I have to do it in the dark.
My grandmother will not move. She has said so in front of everybody, so now she cannot.
We keep the good rope for the ladder and the bad rope for everything else. That is new.
Somebody asked how long we have got out here. The whole room found something else to do.
They are making me memorise which houses were where, out under the water, in order.
Half the houses here are empty and I know which ones. Three of them still have doors that shut.
I collect the good bits of glass off the beach. The sea rubs them soft. I have a jar.
There is a cart with no wheels behind the last house and it is mine now, as a boat.
The gulls take anything you put down for one second. One second. I have tested it.
My job is turning the fish on the racks so they dry evenly. It is boring and it smells.
There is a bell on a post that we ring if we see weather coming. I have never rung it.
The sand gets into the house no matter what anybody does about it, and people still shout.
Somebody left a whole set of pots behind when they moved and we are just using them now.
The beach used to be much wider. There is an old photo of it. It is a completely different beach.
Boats tie up where the carts used to turn round. There is a ring in the wall for each thing.
Every year somebody moves out of the bottom row and up to the top. Nobody moves the other way.
The road out of here goes down and then it goes into the water and then it stops being a road.
We had a garden. It went salty. Now it is where we keep the nets.
My friend's house is empty because her family moved uphill and she had to go with them.
I can tell which house has been empty the longest. It is the one where the weeds are over the handle.
There is a line of dark stone on every wall here at the same height. That is where the water gets.
The house on the corner still has curtains in it and nobody has lived there for years.
There is a name painted on a boat pulled up in the weeds. The family that owned it left.
My mother goes and stands in the empty street sometimes. She does not do anything, she just stands.
We took the door off my grandparents' old house and used it for our table. It is our table now.
There is a doll in the window of number four and everybody has decided to leave it there.
Somebody scratched their height on a doorframe, going up and up, and then it stops.
The bakery oven is still there in the ruin. My father says he can still smell it. He cannot.
My grandmother will not walk down the bottom lane. She goes the long way round. Every time.
A man came through who was walking the whole great wall looking for the break in it. He had bad feet.
They say the pointy markers are for showing where the water stops. So somebody knew, back then.
Every roof beam here is supposedly cut to the same angle as the mountain terrace place. Supposedly.
The pilgrims who go to the calendar stone come back and say it did not say anything.
My uncle argues that the carved city is older than the water and therefore proves something.
The tomb is a tomb for one person and everybody agrees about it, which is the only thing everybody agrees about.
There is a story that lions drank at the arches place. I have never seen a lion. Nobody has.
Wall-walkers stop here for salt and water and then keep going. They are always limping.
We are mid-decision, my mother says. She has said that for four years now.
They are taking the good beams out of the empty houses before the sea gets them.
The families that went up the hill send word back. The word is always: come up.
I have to learn the names of the empty houses and who lived in them, in order along the street.
My father is teaching me to mend a roof I do not think we will still be under.
We planted trees on the high ground this year instead of in the garden. That is a decision.
Somebody is writing a list of everything that has been left behind here, so it is at least written.
There is talk of moving the bell up the hill. Moving the bell would mean it is really over.
My grandmother says she has moved once and once is enough for one life.
Chalk on my hands again. We do sums in the morning and letters after, every day.
My job is the goats. Goats are cleverer than people say and it is a problem.
The terraces have to be weeded on both sides and there are nine of them.
We carry water up. Everything up here has to be carried up, including the water.
There is a plum tree that only fruits on one side. That is the side out of the wind.
It is colder here and everybody keeps saying so as if it is news.
I am learning to copy letters neatly. Neatly is the hard bit. Mine come out slanted.
The wind takes the washing off the line every single time and everybody is surprised.
We are up here because down there went under. That is the whole reason there is a village here.
They write down where the water got to each year, in a book, with the date next to it.
You can see the sea from the top field and it is closer every year, but only a bit.
My family came up in my great-grandmother's time. Everybody's family came up at some point.
The old road comes up the hill and stops at nothing, because the something is under water.
Nobody up here builds low. There is a rule about it and the rule has a number.
The terraces are dug so the rain runs off instead of taking the soil. We copied that from somewhere.
We can see the waterline village from here. They are on sticks. We are on rock.
The ledger has every drowned house in it, the year it went, and who was in it.
It does not say that one of them sang while she gutted fish. Nobody was writing that down.
My great-grandmother carried plum stones up here in her mouth because her hands were full.
Four stones and two trees came up. She is buried under the smaller one, which is the one that fruits.
There are keys hanging by our door for houses that are all underwater now.
We keep a chair that came up from the old house. Nobody sits in it and nobody will move it.
My grandfather can name every family in the low town and what they saved and what they did not.
There is a whole shelf of the ledger for one bad year. One year, one shelf.
Our terraces are copied from the mountain place where they built and did not drown.
Ours are copied badly, my grandfather says, because we copied a drawing of a drawing.
The record keeper argues about the carved city with anybody who sits down at his table.
He says it was carved and not built, so it is older than the water, so the world had a before.
The pointy markers are on high ground, which people say proves they knew where high ground was.
There are people who walk the great wall looking for the break. They come through for supplies.
The calendar stone predicts the water, everybody says. My teacher says it predicts nothing.
The tomb is for one person and it is the most beautiful thing and there is no argument about it.
Everybody is copying books. Two of every book, then four. My hands cramp and I have said so.
We are writing down the names of the drowned villages before the last person who saw them dies.
They planted a whole new orchard this spring. It fruits in nine years. Somebody worked that out.
The seed jars go in the cave where it is cold. Not to eat. To keep.
I have to learn my family backwards, seven people deep, and be able to say it in order.
The lowlanders will come up eventually. We are already deciding where to put them.
My mother says our job is remembering. That is a strange job to be given.
They are teaching everybody letters, even the ones who will never need to write anything.
Somebody asked what all the writing is for. The answer was: for whoever is next.
There was ice on the bucket again this morning and everybody acted surprised again.
Thin soup, thin walls, thin air. That is the joke here and people still make it.
We only wash on the warm days, and the warm days are not that warm.
My job is bringing the animals in before dark and dark comes very early up here.
The path down is two hours. The path up is four. That is the same path.
We burn dung because there are no trees at this height. It smells exactly like you think.
I sleep with the dog for the warmth. My mother pretends not to know about this.
You can see the whole coast from up here and it is a different shape from the old map.
Nobody up here worries about the water, which is the whole reason people came up here.
My family came up two lifetimes ago and everybody still calls us the new ones.
There is an old map nailed to the wall in the hall with a lot of it now wrong.
We are the highest people. If it gets to us, my father says, it has got to everybody.
The traders who come up tell us which villages went under this year. It is a short list. It is never empty.
There is nothing to farm up here, so we keep records instead. That is a real answer people give.
The dead go in the rock because you cannot dig a grave in this ground.
There is a niche in the wall with a comb and a fishing weight and a milk tooth in it.
Nobody labelled them. Somebody put them there and then that somebody died too.
My grandmother came up from a fishing village and has not touched a boat since.
There is a boat up here. On a mountain. Somebody carried it up and nobody knows why.
We have a bowl from a house nobody alive has been inside. We use it. It is a good bowl.
The oldest names in the book are all from the same drowned place, all in one hand.
My grandfather still ties the knots the coast way and he has not seen the coast in fifty years.
We are as high as the mountain terrace place and half as clever, my grandfather says.
Pilgrims come through wanting salt. Always salt, always for the walk along the great wall.
They are looking for the break where the wall let the sea through. They have been looking for generations.
There is no break, my mother says quietly, and never says it when they are in the room.
The pointy markers stand on high ground. So do we. My father makes a lot of that.
Somebody up here has a drawing of the carved city and charges to look at it.
The calendar stone is supposed to say when it stops. Every pilgrim reads it differently.
The tomb is the one they all agree on. Even the arguing ones go quiet about the tomb.
We take in the ones who come up. There is a room kept ready and it is never empty for long.
The record book has run out of pages twice and they have made more pages both times.
I am learning to read the old hand, the hard one, so the oldest pages do not go silent.
They are copying the books into two sets and one set goes deep into the cave.
My mother says we are the memory. She says it like a job, not like a comfort.
Everybody who arrives here has left something. Nobody asks what. That is the rule.
We are planting trees at this height for the first time. Nobody knows if they will take.
The oldest man here says he wants to be carried down to see the sea once. Nobody has said yes.
It is the same temperature in here always. Outside changes. In here does not.
I am not allowed past the third lamp. The third lamp is where the floor starts sloping.
There are jars along the wall taller than me and I am not to touch them, so I count them.
Forty-one jars. I have counted it wrong before, so it might be forty-one.
Water drips into a stone basin all night and fills it by morning. Every morning.
My job is the lamps. Trimming them. The smoke goes along the roof in a black stripe.
The floor in the front chamber has been swept so long it has gone dished in the middle.
People have lived in here longer than anywhere. Longer than the villages. Much longer.
The old entrance is under the water now. The fish go in and out of it.
We put things in here that we want to keep dry, and dry is getting harder to find.
There is a mark on the wall for the water each year, but the water is nowhere near.
They moved the seed jars deeper in after a wet winter. Deeper is drier.
This is where things come when the low villages give up on them.
The stone stays the same. That is why everybody keeps saying the stone stays the same.
Everybody's grandparents' things end up in here eventually. Ours are on the fourth shelf.
The dead are in the fourth chamber with their feet towards the entrance. All of them.
The oldest ones are deepest in. So you walk backwards through everybody as you go.
There is a niche with a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth in it and no name.
The writing on the jars goes neat, neat, neat, and then it goes different. Somebody new started doing it.
That means the person writing them stopped, and somebody else carried on. Nobody says who.
There is a bowl worn into the stone where the drip lands. That took a very long time.
My grandmother's name is on a jar. She filled it. It is still sealed.
Books are stacked spine out in the dry chamber. The ones about the sea are worn to nothing.
There are handprints along the low passage, at the height of a grown-up walking.
Somebody painted seven shapes in a row on the deep wall: a triangle, a long line, a ring of arches.
The triangle is the pointy markers and the long line is the great wall. Everybody agrees that much.
There is a charcoal drawing of the ring of arches with a water line ruled straight across it.
The arguments about the carved city happen down here because the echo makes everyone sound certain.
Carved, not built. Say it in the dark and it comes back sounding like proof.
There is a calendar of small squares cut into the rock by the entrance. The squares run out.
Whoever was cutting them stopped four winters ago. Nobody has picked it back up.
They put my handprint on the wall next to all the old ones. Mine is the smallest by a lot.
The seed jars are in two sets now. One set is sealed with wax and stands right at the back.
The back set is not for us. Nobody will say who it is for, but it is not for us.
There is a new shelf, planed smooth and pegged in, completely empty, built to fit books.
The copying happens down here where it is dry. Two of every book, then four.
My mother says everything worth keeping ends up in the rock eventually, including us.
They are teaching me to find my way out of here in the dark. That is a lesson now.
Somebody asked what all of this is being kept for. My grandfather said: for after.
